slidelink.displaytext: The Manufacture of the Various Types of Amorphous Silica
Basic Manufacturing Process for Silica Gel
Formation of Primary Silica Gel Structure
Porosity Mapping of Silica Gel Products

search.slidetext: this course contains audio narration. you can use the controls at the bottom of the screen to control the volume, pause, and replay the audio. okay okay okay okay okay okay silica gel 101 welcome to the silica gel platform technologies introduction module. in this course, we’ll discuss the properties and manufacturing process of silica gel and explore what makes it such a vital part of grace’s product portfolio. let’s start by exploring what silica gel is.

what is silica gel? chemical properties chemical properties physical properties physical properties nontoxic highly pure the surface hydroxyl groups can be present in a large total number because of the high surface area hydroxyl groups are hydrophilic and readily hydrogen bond hydroxyl groups are weaker acids than acetic acid chemically stable (especially at low ph) non-crystalline no absorbance in visible light spectrum refractive index of 1.46, matching many organic systems electrically insulating thermally stable high hardness continuum of particle structures low solubility when you heard silica, you may have thought of sand. silica is a naturally occurring oxide of silicon and a main component of several minerals, and yes, sand. but silica doesn’t just occur in nature. it’s also possible to create it in the laboratory so we can adjust certain properties, such as pore size. grace produces synthetic amorphous silica that is a remarkable material for many reasons that involve its chemical and physical properties. silica gel is just one of the forms of silica that grace produces; we also produce colloidal and precipitated silicas. let’s look at several of these properties. chemically, amorphous silica is nontoxic. in fact, it is approved as a food additive. and through grace’s manufacturing process, it can be made with high purity. at the surface of silica particles, the silicate network is terminated with hydroxyl groups that are slightly acidic. these surface hydroxyl groups can be present in a large total number because of the high surface area of typical commercial silica. it is non-crystalline, so health concerns that pertain to crystalline silicas don’t apply. for the most part, amorphous silica does not absorb light in the visible light spectrum, and the refractive index matches many organic systems, so optically transparent mixes and films can be prepared. it is electrically and thermally insulating, and it has high hardness, which is important in abrasive applications. from a structural point of view, silica gel is a porous material, and the porosity can be varied across a continuum of properties.

silica gel properties and manufacturing now that we have a basic understanding of what makes synthetic amorphous silica special and some of the key properties of silica gel, let’s discuss the specific properties of silica gel and the manufacturing process grace follows to develop these properties.

morphology differences between amorphous silicas common precursor: sodium silicate silica gel family structural analogy: sponge gel: aggregation and polymerization colloidal family structural analogy: individual grapes colloidal: nucleation and growth precipitated family structural analogy: cluster of grapes precipitated: hybrid of gel and colloidal silica gel, as the name implies, has a gel-like structure. that is, the silica network is composed of interconnecting chains of silicate species, and when synthesized, these chains trap the water used in the reaction. when the water is removed, a highly porous, uniformly cross-linked structure remains. the uniformity of the silicate backbone is key for creating uniformly sized pores. although the structure of amorphous silica gel is difficult to describe, theoretical models have shown primary particles of silica, initially about one-point-five nanometers in diameter, bonding with each other to form a three-dimensional interconnected network. we use subsequent processing to modify the original structure and create the possible end products. at the other end of the spectrum is colloidal silica. these particles are produced by the nucleation of a silicate species, followed by controlled growth of the nuclei. by careful control of both the nucleation and growth processes, we can synthesize particles with very narrow and monomodal particle size distributions. the primary particles are themselves nonporous. if we attend to the requirements of the surface colloid chemistry of the particles, they appear as relatively concentrated dispersions in water. additionally, they do not sediment because of their very small size. finally, precipitated silica can be considered a kind of structural intermediate between silica gel and colloidal silica. during the synthesis of precipitated silica, we can nucleate and grow particles, which are then agglomerated to form weak aggregates. if we imagine silica particles like grapes, structurally, colloidal silica particles might look like individual grapes, while precipitated silica would be like a cluster of grapes. it is possible to vary the particle size during precipitated silica synthesis, and this is the primary means of controlling the surface area and porosity. so continuing with our grape analogy, silica gel would be like very small grapes that have been strongly bonded together to form a three-dimensional network.

the manufacture of the various types of amorphous silica all three of the major types of amorphous silica have a common precursor—sodium silicate. the initial manufacturing steps all involve creating silicic acid molecules and a small silicate species called micelles. from that point, the micelles can either aggregate together (creating silica gel), grow (creating colloidal silica), or do a combination of both (creating precipitated silica). the manufacturing process and specific conditions determine how the micelles will interact with each other and, subsequently, what type of silica will be formed.

this is an interactive slide. %intro_instructions% each element on this slide to continue. continue continue continue continue continue continue overall reaction stoichiometry: na2sio3 + h2so4 sio2 + h2o + na2so4 representation of silica condensation: si(oh)4 + si(oh)4 (oh)3si-o-si(oh)3 + h2o basic manufacturing process for silica gel sodium silicate sodium silicate mineral acid mix mix hydrosol (liquid) hydrogel (solid) wash/modify wash/modify hydrous gels hydrous gels xerogels xerogels aerogels aerogels size reduction size reduction fine size silica we distinguish the various forms of amorphous silica by the processes by which they are made. in the case of silica gel, it’s made by rapidly mixing sodium silicate and a slight stoichiometric excess of sulfuric acid. the sodium sulfate must be removed by a wash step, and we can further modify the structure depending on the wash conditions, such as time, temperature, and ph. finally, once the silica gel has been appropriately modified, it is dried to varying degrees and then milled to various target final particle sizes.

solution precursor—sodium silicate the starting material from which we form particles is complex itself. recent work has led to a phase diagram for the silica species that lumps the species beyond silica monomers into proto-particles. ~0.25 nm 1 2 3 4 5 the starting material from which we form particles is complex. recent work from the university of delaware has led to a phase diagram for the silica species that lumps the species beyond silica monomers into proto-particles, with either fully protonated or partially deprotonated hydroxyl groups. we can see that, prior to reaction with acid, the silicate system is clearly mostly particulate in nature. note that these particles are very small—one-point-five nanometers or less.

mixing the acid neutralizes the highly alkaline silicate. this produces sodium sulfate as a reaction byproduct. after the silicate is neutralized, a self-condensation reaction begins and produces water as a byproduct. in early stages of the reaction, the mixture remains a liquid. as the reaction continues, the viscosity of the mix increases and eventually solidifies. representation of silica condensation: si(oh)4 + si(oh)4 (oh)3si-o-si(oh)3 + h2o the acid neutralizes the highly alkaline silicate and produces sodium sulfate as a reaction byproduct. once the silicate is neutralized, a self-condensation reaction begins, and this reaction produces water as a byproduct. in the early stages of the reaction, the mixture remains a liquid and is called a hydrosol. as the reaction advances, the molecular weight of the silica oligomers increases to the point at which the viscosity of the mix increases dramatically and the mix solidifies. at this point, the mixture is called a hydrogel.

formation of primary silica gel structure iler promoted the view of formed silica gel as having a structure that was at least partially particulate in nature. the model can account for surface area and pore volume of gels based on the size and coordination number of the primary particles. iler promoted the view of formed silica gel as having a structure that was at least partially particulate in nature. this model could account for the surface area and pore volume of processed gels on the basis of the size and the coordination number of the primary particles. the coordination number refers to how densely packed the micelles are— or how many nearest neighbors each particle has. measured surface area is considered to come from the primary particles, and the pore volume comes from the voids between the primary particles. the surface areas of final gels range from about 300 to 700 meters squared per gram with pore volumes that range from about point four to two centimeters cubed per gram. these structures are formed from primary particles that ranged from about 4 to 9 nanometers, with the coordination ranging from about 6 to a little less than 4.

monomer-cluster cluster-cluster reaction-limited ballistic diffusion-limited d = 3.00 d = 3.00 d = 3.00 d = 1.95 d = 2.50 d = 1.80 formation of secondary structures work in the late 1980s and 1990s shed more light on how the fractal nature of materials affect the formation of silica gels. based on the conditions, the primary particles aggregate to form secondary structures. the shape of the secondary structures depends on whether or not the primary particles stick together immediately (called diffusion-limited aggregation), or whether they can bounce off and re-form over and over again to form dense structures. similarly, if there are clusters of particles in the system (such as the oligomers in the starting silicate), these preformed clusters can also show a range of different shapes. the d value shown in the graphic is the fractal dimension, which is 3 for euclidean objects (like a solid sphere) and is less than 3 for shapes that have some fractal character. for spherical and dense particles, the mass varies as the third power of the radius, and so the fractal dimension is 3. for freshly synthesized silica gel, the fractal dimension is about 2, so that the particle mass varies roughly as the square of the particle radius.

salt removal after the initial reaction of the gel, there are many sulfate and sodium ions in the pores of the silica. the goal of washing is to remove these atoms. at a ph above 7, the silica surface carries a slightly negative charge, so some of the positively charged salts are needed to balance the negatively charged surface. at a low ph, there is no net charge. at these ph levels, the residual sodium is easier to remove. h h h o o- si na+ o o o o o o si si si si o- na+ sodium ion-exchanged onto the silica gel surface at alkaline ph. after the initial reaction of the silica gel, there are many sulfate and sodium ions within the pores of the silica. the goal of washing the silica gel is to remove these unnecessary atoms. the sodium and sulfates contained within the silica are mostly present as a salt. however, at a ph above about 7, the silica surface carries a slightly negative charge, so some of the positively charged sodium is needed to balance the negatively charged surface. this sodium is difficult to remove. interestingly, the charge on the silica surface depends on ph so that at a low ph (in fact ph 3), there is no net charge. at that ph, then, the residual sodium is easy to remove. that’s why most silica gel grades have a wash step at low ph to remove most of the sodium.

aging pore modifications can occur in wash cycles through aging. the fresh gel is aged with ammonia at a high temperature for varying amounts of time. even though the solubility of silica is relatively low, it is soluble to an extent that depends on temperature and ph. solubility of amorphous silica—ppm ph pore modification can occur during wash cycles via aging. this means that the fresh gel is aged with ammonia (at a high ph) and at a high temperature, for varying amounts of time. let’s look closer at the chemical and physical transformations that must occur to achieve the wide range of porosities. the first consideration involves the solubility of amorphous silica. even though the solubility of silica is relatively low, it is soluble in water to an extent that depends on temperature and ph. for example, if silica gel is treated at high temperatures and a high ph, the solubility increases substantially. this chemistry can be exploited to change the structure of the silica gel.

ostwald ripening %intro_instructions% to replay animation. for thermodynamic reasons, for very small particles (such as the one-point-five nanometer micelles in silica gel), solubility is a function of the radius of curvature of the particle. so if the curvature is convex, the solubility is relatively high, while if the curvature is concave, the solubility is correspondingly low. if the solubility is high enough, the material will dissolve from the region of positive curvature. but if the solubility is not too high, the dissolved material will precipitate at the region of negative curvature. this process is called ostwald ripening. generally, this process results in a loss of surface area, but it can also result in an increase in the mechanical strength of the gel as well as an increase in the porosity of the gel. this chemistry generally occurs during the wash steps of the freshly made gel.

drying after the salts and sodium are mostly removed by washing and the structure modified by aging, or ostwald ripening, the structure is further modified by the drying conditions. when the gel is dried, the water that fills the internal pores must be removed. water is a relatively high-surface-tension fluid, and as a result, when the water recedes into the pores, a meniscus is created. the surface tension associated with this meniscus exerts a force on the walls of the gel that tends to draw it inward. the extent of the pore deformation depends on the stability of the silicate structure. if the gel network is not strong enough to resist this force, the structure will collapse, resulting in low internal pore volume. but if the network is strong enough to resist the collapse, a high-pore-volume product can be achieved. %intro_instructions% to replay animation.

hydrogels, aerogels, and xerogels surface dry hydrous gel if a hydrous gel is overdried, shrinkage will occur over time (hours or days), resulting in lower oil adsorption and higher water activity partially dry fully dry aerogel(fast drying time) xerogel(slow drying time) finally, one other element of structural complexity occurs during drying. the extent of the shrinkage of the gel network as the meniscus recedes during drying also depends on how fast the water is removed. if the water is removed very quickly, as in flash drying, the gel network doesn’t have enough time to shrink. grace terms these products as fast-drying aerogels, and they have the highest pore volumes. if the water is removed very slowly, then the gel network has plenty of time to shrink. these products are referred to as xerogels at grace, and they have relatively low pore volume. finally, hydrogel gel products—which are supplied with water still in the pores—can display an interesting phenomenon associated with shrinkage during drying. if the products are overdried so that the meniscus lies inside the pores, the particle can respond by shrinking over time.

milling grace uses two different milling technologies: air classifying mills (acms) and fluid energy mills (fems). the acm is a hammer mill where size reduction occurs by particle-to-wall collisions. this process yields particles from 12 to 50 microns. the fem is a spiral jet mill. here, size reduction occurs by particle-to-particle collisions. this produces much smaller particles (from 3 to 15 microns). silica particles can be wet milled in a liquid phase (typically water) to achieve submicron sizes. the particle size of the silica gel product is an important property. available sizes span the range from submicron size to several millimeters. the type of milling unit operation determines both the size of the final product as well as the width of the distribution. for very large products, we use a granulation process. to achieve particles that are above about 10 microns, we use air classifier mills. smaller micronized grades, in the range of about 3 microns to about 15 microns, can be produced using fluid energy mills. we can produce particles that are submicron in size in dispersions by fine media milling operations.

silica gel porosity as you’ve learned, one of the key properties of silica gel is its porosity. at grace, we are experts in adjusting the porosity of the silica gel to create the precise porosity for the specific application of the silica gel.

porosity dense silica particle (micelle) pore volume = 0 cm3/g particle density = 2.15 g/cm3 porous silica particle pore volume = 1.8 cm3/g particle density = 0.44 g/cm3 pore volume = 1.8 cm3/g particle density = 0.44 g/cm3 pore volume = 0 cm3/g particle density = 2.15 g/cm3 the porosity of amorphous silica gel has three components: pore volume, surface area, and pore diameter. the particle on the left represents a nonporous silica particle, such as in colloidal silica and as in the one-point-five nanometer micelle that is the primary particle for silica gel. these dense particles have a density of about two-point-one-five grams per centimeters cubed. by comparison, the particle on the right shows the distinction between the pore diameter, the internal surface area, the external particle surface area, and the pore volume. by carefully controlling the manufacturing process, we can vary the porosity of amorphous silica gel over a wide range.

measuring porosity at low partial pressure, nitrogen adsorbs in a monolayer on the surface. used to calculate the brunauer–emmett–teller (bet) surface area at high partial pressure, nitrogen condenses in the pores. used to calculate the barrett–joyner–halenda (bjh) pore volume pore diameter can be calculated using the following: apd (å) = 4 x 104 * pv (cm3/g)/sa (m2/g) there are several methods for measuring the surface area and pore volume of the particles. the most common method we use is nitrogen porosimetry. at low partial pressure, nitrogen adsorbs in a monolayer on the surface of the particle. this information is used to calculate the surface area. then at a high partial pressure, nitrogen condenses in the pores, and from this, we calculate the pore volume. from the surface area and pore volume, the pore diameter can be calculated using this equation: additional methods for measuring the surface area and pore volume are mercury porosimetry and oil absorption.

pore size distribution the pore size distribution is an important consideration. we can distinguish between different types of materials by the nature of the distribution. crystalline zeolite-type materials are microporous, and they are characterized by a very sharp pore size distribution— typically around a few angstroms in diameter. silica gel pore size distributions are also well defined; although the size and the width depend on the particle structure. the pore structure of precipitated silica, which is made by an entirely different process, is not well defined, and pores in that material can span a wide range from very small to very large.

porosity mapping of silica gel products this graph provides a useful map for showing the range of porosities of our commercial products. the map also shows how the porosity of the silica gel determines which applications it can be used for. for example, the blue polygon encompasses an area of relatively high-surface-area, low-pore-volume products, and these are typically used in desiccant applications. at the other end of the map, the light tan polygon encompasses an area of relatively low surface area and high pore volume, and these products are typically used in thickening applications. many matting agents also have high pore volume and low surface area, because for the matting application, a low-particle density is desired. since the matting effect is accomplished by particles, the low-particle density enables a high matting effect to be achieved with a minimal mass of particles. low-surface-area, low-pore-volume particles are relatively hard, and these particles are typically used in abrasive applications, such as for cleaning in toothpaste. gels with intermediate surface area and pore volume are useful in chromatographic separations. desiccation or adsorption high sa, low pd 0 200 400 600 800 1000 1200 1400 0 0.5 1 1.5 2 2.5 3 25a 50a 75a 100a 125a 150a 175a 200a 225a surface area [m2/g] pore volume [cm3/g] graphic: neil pryor abrasion and cleaning low pv chromatography and purification high pd matting thickening high pv
surface chemistry the surface chemistry of the silica gel is another key property. let’s look deeper into this chemistry to see how it works.

this is an interactive slide. %intro_instructions% each element on this slide to continue. continue continue continue continue continue continue in water, the surface will become ionized. can hydrogen bond with donor groups. can covalently bond or be functionalized with various chemistries. surface chemistry basics hydroxyl groups hydroxyl groups hydroxyl groups hydroxyl groups electrostatic properties electrostatic properties electrostatic properties electrostatic properties %intro_instructions% each tab to continue. surface silanol groups are somewhat acidic, and when they are in aqueous media, they will deprotonate to an extent that depends on ph. at high ph, the deprotonation reaction is driven to the right, and the surface develops a negative charge; in acidic media, the reaction is driven to the left, and the surface will be fully hydroxylated, with neutral charge. select each tab to learn more.

basic chemistry of hydroxyl groups the silanol (or hydroxyl) groups are very hydrophilic, and they will interact with additives that are capable of hydrogen bonding, such as with water. water can be present in molecular form on the surface of the silica through the hydrogen bonding interaction, and we refer to this as physically bound water. we can remove physically bound water by application of relatively low-temperature heat. adjacent silanol groups can also undergo a reaction that produces water as a byproduct, with the result being additional silicon-oxygen bonds. we call this type of water chemically bound water. it is more difficult to remove, and the reaction occurs at higher temperatures than the removal of physically bound water. h h o o si o o o o o o si si si si o h h h h o chemically bound water physically bound water

rad 2105 syloid® 74 water cyclohexane surface energy the surface of silica has a surface tension (or energy); important for wetting and adhesion. surface energy can be measured and analyzed as having two components—polar and dispersive. polar and nonpolar solvents and polymers will wet the high energy silica surface. wetting issues are kinetic, not chemical. the surface has a surface tension or energy, which is important for wetting and adhesion. we can measure and analyze the surface energy as having two components—polar and dispersive. we base the energy of immersion of the powders in liquids on this information. polar and nonpolar solvents and polymers will wet the high energy silica surface—this is thermodynamically favorable. waxes will also wet the silica surface. wetting issues are kinetic, not chemical—for example, highly viscous liquids taking time to flow into the pore. in the bar graph, you’ll see the immersion energy of two grades, a non-wax grade (syloid® 74) and a wax grade (syloid® rad 2105), in two different solvents (polar water and nonpolar cyclohexane). a negative energy of immersion means there is a favorable interaction energy, meaning that the sample will disperse spontaneously in the solvent. both powders will wet spontaneously in both solvents separately. however, the magnitude of the energies is different. the syloid® 74 has a much stronger interaction with water than the rad 2105. thus, when subjected to a mixture of water and cyclohexane, the syloid® 74 will partition into the water phase. by comparison, the rad 2105 has a much stronger energy of immersion with the cyclohexane so that in a mixture of the two solvents, it will partition into the cyclohexane. the cyclohexane is less dense than the water, and so it is the top layer in the picture. the rad 2105, with its pores filled with cyclohexane, is a little denser than the solvent itself, so it settles at the bottom of the cyclohexane layer.

summary the various forms of amorphous silica are distinguished by the processes by which they are made. in the case of silica gel, sodium silicate and a slight stoichiometric excess of sulfuric acid are rapidly mixed. the sodium sulfate must be removed by a wash step, and further modification can occur depending on the wash conditions. once the silica gel has been appropriately modified, it is dried to varying degrees and then milled to various target final particle sizes. the pore structure and particle size, as well as the surface chemistry, are all key functionalities in the many applications of silica gel. in summary, we categorize the various forms of amorphous silica by the processes by which they are made. in the case of silica gel, sodium silicate and a slight stoichiometric excess of sulfuric acid are rapidly mixed. the sodium sulfate must be removed by a wash step, and further structure modification can occur depending on the wash conditions such as time, temperature, and ph. finally, once we have appropriately modified the silica gel, we dry it to varying degrees and then mill it to various target final particle sizes. the pore structure and particle size, as well as the surface chemistry, are all key functionalities in the many applications of silica gel.
